The Rippling Mere of Vesper Tide

At the heart of an enchanted grove lies the Rippling Mere, where a druid strikes the water with her staff to call the spirits below. Each strike sends a ring racing outward across the water at a steady pace — the Vesper Tide (v) — how fast the ripple itself travels across the mere.

The druid taps her staff again and again, sending out new ripples — the Fathom-beat (f) — how many ripples she sends out every second.

Between one strike and the next, a certain time always passes — the Tollbell Turn (T) — the time for one complete ripple to form and settle, start to finish.

Out on the water, the crest of one ripple to the crest of the very next is always the same distance apart — the Lakespan (λ).

And how high each ripple rises above the mere's still surface — measured only from flat water up to the crest, never trough to crest — is the Ardent Swell (A).

Strike harder, and the Ardent Swell grows taller, though the Vesper Tide never changes; strike faster, and the Fathom-beat quickens while the Tollbell Turn shortens to match — always partners, one the flip side of the other.

The dashed vertical line is a fixed point in space — a way to count how many waves pass it each second.

The Harp of Ninefold Echoes

In a bard's workshop hangs an ancient harp, its single enchanted string stretched taut between two silver pegs. The distance between those pegs is the Loomspan (L).

When the bard plucks the string just right, it splits into a pattern of shimmering loops, each with a perfectly still point where the string barely moves at all. The count of that pattern — one loop for the fundamental hum, two for the first true harmony — is the Nodefall Count (n).

Pluck it to sing with one great loop, and you hear the harp's deepest, truest note. Coax it into two loops instead, and the note leaps higher — same string, same Loomspan, different Nodefall Count entirely.

How taut the bard keeps that string is its Heartcord Strain (T) — tighten it, and the ripples race along the string faster, lifting every note it sings. And how much of the string itself is packed into each hand's-span of its length is the Warpweight (μ) — a thick, heavy-wound bass string carries the ripple slower than a thin one strung to the very same tightness, singing a deeper note as a result.

The dots mark the nodes — points on the string that never move.

The Herald's Ride

A royal herald gallops toward the castle gates, blowing a horn to announce the king's return. Struck at rest, that horn always sounds the exact same true note — the Forgesong (f), the pitch as it was forged, untouched by motion.

The guards atop the wall don't hear the Forgesong — they hear the Farhearing (f'), the pitch that actually reaches their ears, climbing higher as the herald draws near and dropping low the moment he thunders past.

How fast the herald gallops toward the gate is the Vanguard's Pace (vS) — the faster that pace, the more the Farhearing bends away from the true Forgesong.

If a guard leaves her post and runs out to meet him instead, her own running speed becomes the Vantage Drift (vo) — running toward the sound bends the pitch higher too, just as surely as the herald's galloping does.

All of this — the Forgesong bending into the Farhearing — happens through the still evening air itself, which carries every sound at its own steady pace: the Windcarry (vW). It never changes no matter how the herald rides or the guard runs; only their paces relative to the Windcarry decide how far the pitch bends.

Wavefronts bunch up ahead of the source and spread out behind it — that bunching is the whole effect.

The Rival Fiddlers of Twinmoor

At the festival of Twinmoor, two enchanted fiddlers sound together. The fiddle of the best bard (Fantasia the First, daughter of Figaro the tuneful) lets out a steady note — the 1st Fiddle (f1).

Tired of always being 2nd fiddle, Foghorn the 2nd (son of Foghorn the truly tuneless), a rival bard, tries to match it exactly — (f2).

When the two are almost — but not quite — in tune, the combined sound throbs: swelling loud, then fading soft, over and over. That throbbing pulse is the Discord Throb (Δf) — the crowd counts how many times it swells each second to know how far out of tune the fiddles (well, let's be honest, Foghorn) really are. They're keen to get it right — they get to throw that many rotten enchantoes at him.

Desperate to avoid the rain of rotten enchanted tomatoes, Foghorn the 2nd tunes closer to the first, the Discord Throb slows... and slows... until it vanishes entirely, and the two fiddles sound as one. The crowd boos — they're really just here for the rotten fruit.

The dashed outline is the beat envelope — the "loud...quiet...loud" pattern you'd actually hear.

The Golden Sanctum

A single amber pane of the Sunspire window — unmixed, pure — lets through one true wavelength of honeyed light. That golden beam falls on the wall of Rune-Gates, passes through both slits spaced by the Duskgate Divide (d), and crosses the chamber to the Lantern Reach (L) beyond.

Where the two golden beams overlap, they weave into alternating bands of rich amber light and shadow — the Xyrindel Bands (x) — evenly spaced from one edge of the Reach to the other, every stripe the same warm gold as the last.

Because the light is pure, every Band is identical: same brightness, same hue, same spacing. Narrow the Duskgate Divide and the Bands crowd closer together; widen the Lantern Reach and they spread further apart — exactly what x = λL/d predicts, no surprises.

Each Xyrindel Band can also be given its place in line — the Sunspire Rank (n) — counting outward from the golden heart of the pattern, where the central Band is Rank Zero. The angle at which a beam bends away from that central line before striking a given Band is its Halo Bearing (θ); the extra distance one golden beam must travel past its twin to reach that same Band is the Twinbeam Reckoning (Δ) — and for every Band that glows bright, the Twinbeam Reckoning always comes out to a whole number of golden wavelengths, never a fraction of one.

Each glowing band on the right is a bright fringe — evenly spaced, like a barcode.

The Watchgate of Whispering Keep

Deep in Whispering Keep stands a single ancient gate — the only way in or out for any sound, light, or spell. How wide that gate is cut, jamb to jamb, is the Watchgate's Width (w).

Cut the Watchgate narrow, close to the size of whatever wave tries to pass through, and that wave spreads out wildly on the far side, bending into every corner of the courtyard beyond. Cut it wide instead, and the wave barely bends at all, marching straight through as if the gate weren't there.

The narrower the Watchgate relative to what's passing through it, the more everything on the other side spreads out and whispers into every shadow.

A narrow gap spreads the wave out wide; a wide gap barely bends it at all.

These formulae are NOT printed on the real AS91523 Resource Booklet — unlike every other formula in this app, you have to know these cold, from memory, on exam day.

Standing waves — open pipe or string

λ = 2L / n

n = 1, 2, 3, ... (every harmonic is possible). Both ends are nodes (string fixed at both ends) or antinodes (pipe open at both ends).

Standing waves — closed pipe

λ = 4L / n

n = 1, 3, 5, ... ODD harmonics only. One end is a node (closed end), the other an antinode (open end).

Beat frequency

Δf = |f1 − f2|

The rate at which two almost-matching notes pulse loud-soft-loud as they drift in and out of step with each other.
